title: Vipassi's four sights
hook: the story of a past Buddha, Vipassi, who also saw the four sights

segments.voice: Yesterday: a mind of goodwill heard in every direction, and your line, the note isn't forced. Who heard your quiet note? Today, a story you may think you already know, told about someone else. Day five hundred forty-three.

A prince rides out of the palace to the royal park. On the road his charioteer slows down. There's a man by the road, bent over, gray, leaning on a stick. What's wrong with him? the prince asks. He's old, the charioteer says. Will I get old? Everyone does, sir. The prince turns the chariot around and goes home, shaken. Most people know this scene as the young Siddhattha's. But in the oldest detailed telling in the Pali canon, the prince in the chariot has a different name. Today: Vipassi's four sights.
screen: `AN OLD MAN BY THE ROAD.` → `WILL I GET OLD?` → `A DIFFERENT PRINCE.`

segments.voice: The fourteenth Long Discourse, the Mahapadana, the great story, begins with monks chatting about past lives. The Buddha joins them and names six Buddhas before himself, going back ninety-one aeons to the first, Vipassi. Then he tells Vipassi's life in full. The pattern is striking. Vipassi's father, King Bandhuma, hears a prediction that his son will either rule the world or leave it. So he surrounds him with pleasures. Then, on four separate trips to the park, Vipassi sees an old man, then a sick man, then a dead man carried out with mourners, and each time he turns back troubled, and each time his father adds more pleasures. On the fourth trip he sees a shaven-headed wanderer in a robe. What is he? A man who has gone forth, sir, who lives kindly and harmlessly. Vipassi goes forth. Alone, he reflects: this world has fallen into trouble. It's born, it ages, it dies. And how does anyone escape? He traces the conditions back, link by link, and awakens. Even his hesitation to teach is there, and a Brahma who asks him to. The sutta calls this kind of pattern dhammata, the way things are for every Buddha. In the canon, the four sights are told in detail of Vipassi; later biographies tell the same scene of Gotama, the Buddha of our age. Why tell it this way? Because the point isn't one remarkable prince. The point is that whenever anyone looks clearly at aging, sickness and death, the same questions rise. It happens again.
screen: `SEVEN BUDDHAS, VIPASSI THE FIRST.` · `OLD, SICK, DEAD, A WANDERER.` · `THE SAME PATTERN EVERY TIME.` · `ANYONE WHO LOOKS ASKS AGAIN.` · then, large: `IT HAPPENS AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the four sights come one at a time. First, someone old you know: let their face be clear. Then someone who is sick, or was. Then someone who has died. Don't hurry past any of them. And then a fourth picture: someone calm, someone who has made peace with some of this. Rest with that last face. The questions Vipassi asked are yours to ask too, if you want them. The bell holds the time.
Vipassi, the first Buddha named in the Mahapadana Sutta, who saw age, sickness, death and a wanderer, a pattern later told of Gotama too. Today's word.

Your line: it happens again. Today, when you notice something aging, breaking or ending, remember that people have stood exactly here before you, and asked the same question. Day five hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists honor seven Buddhas of the past, from Vipassi to Gotama, in chants such as the Atanatiya verses, and the four sights are retold in temples, festivals and art across the Buddhist world.

fork.setup: you're Prince Vipassi. on the road to the park you see a man bent with age, and learn that you will age too. what do you do?
options: carry on to the park and enjoy the day.
turn the chariot around and go home, troubled.
leave the palace that very hour.
fork.reveal: he turns back troubled. his father answers by adding more pleasures. only after the fourth sight does Vipassi go forth.

original.note: Pali Vipassi: the name of the first Buddha named in DN 14. it is often heard as clear-seeing.

trapdoor: what you thought: the four sights happened once, to Siddhattha.
what it means: the Mahapadana tells them of Vipassi, as a pattern that recurs for every Buddha.
what a scholar hears: DN 14 is the canonical source of the full four-sights narrative; later biographies such as the Nidanakatha apply it to Gotama.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 14 (Mahapadana Sutta), the seven Buddhas and Vipassi's life
